c.tagline: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, rebuilding around its ancient citadel and souqs.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree the fare with the driver before departing or have your hotel arrange the ride. Shared microbuses (servees) running fixed routes are the cheapest option. Fares are paid in cash, and US dollars are often accepted or preferred alongside Syrian pounds.

emergency.note: 112 reaches police and 110 the ambulance service; dispatchers may not speak English, so ask hotel staff to help. Emergency infrastructure is still being rebuilt after the war.

avoid.reason: Avoid the heavily damaged former front-line districts of eastern Aleppo, where rubble and unexploded ordnance remain, and stay away from military installations; most governments advise against all travel to Syria.
Expect frequent checkpoints, never photograph soldiers or government buildings, and stay on well-trodden paths because of unexploded ordnance.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed walled old town, dominated by the great medieval Citadel of Aleppo and threaded with the covered lanes of Al-Madina Souq, the Great Umayyad Mosque, khans, and hammams; much is undergoing post-war reconstruction, but restored courtyard houses now serve as boutique hotels. Best for travelers who want to be inside Aleppo's ancient core.

The historic Christian quarter just north of the old city, a warren of narrow alleys, ornate courtyard mansions, churches, and Syrian-Ottoman facades, now home to some of the city's atmospheric boutique hotels, cafes, and restaurants; suits travelers wanting heritage character and evening dining.
A leafy central district of early-20th-century buildings, including the storied Baron Hotel, plus mid-range hotels, shops, and restaurants; a practical, relatively lively base close to the old city.

The newer residential and university districts spreading west, with wider streets, apartment blocks, larger hotels, and everyday services; quieter and more spread out, suited to longer or business-oriented stays.

water.note: War-damaged infrastructure makes supply intermittent; drink bottled water only.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor; there is no smart card or app-based ticketing. Fares are very low, and US dollars are commonly used alongside Syrian pounds.
transit.hours: Buses and microbuses run roughly 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM; taxis fill in for later travel.
transit.note: Aleppo has no metro or tram; the city relies on state buses and shared microbuses (servees) on fixed routes, supplemented heavily by taxis, as services continue to be rebuilt after the war.

train: Aleppo (Baghdad) Railway Station - long-distance passenger rail is largely suspended and being restored after war damage
bus: Aleppo main bus/microbus stations with intercity coaches to Damascus, Hama, Homs, and Latakia

airport.name: Aleppo International Airport (ALP)
rentals: Local agencies at the arrivals hall (major international chains are not currently operating)

transit.m: Taxi to the city center (20-25 min) — the most reliable option; agree the fare before departing
Microbus/servees toward central Aleppo where available

tip.r: Rounding up and leaving around 5-10% at restaurants is customary; small tips to drivers, porters, and guides are appreciated. Cash only, and small US-dollar notes are welcome.

food.name: Kebab Karaz (Cherry Kebab)
food.desc: Aleppo's signature dish: small lamb meatballs simmered in tart sour-cherry sauce, served over flatbread with pine nuts and parsley.

places.name: Beit Sissi
places.note: Landmark courtyard mansion restaurant in the Christian quarter, long the classic address for cherry kebab.

places.name: Beit Wakil
places.note: Restored 16th-century house hotel serving old-Aleppo cooking in a stone courtyard.

places.name: Al-Kommeh
places.note: Chef-run Aleppian kitchen that reopened after the war and revived heritage recipes.

food.name: Muhammara
food.desc: Aleppo's famous red dip of roasted pepper, walnut, breadcrumb and pomegranate molasses, scooped with warm bread as part of the mezze spread.

places.name: Beit Wakil
places.note: Full Aleppian mezze table where muhammara arrives alongside a dozen small plates.

places.name: Yasmeen House
places.note: Courtyard house restaurant popular with returning locals for classic mezze.

places.name: Souq al-Attarine spice stalls
places.note: Buy Aleppo pepper, walnuts and pomegranate molasses at the source in the rebuilt spice souq.

food.name: Kibbeh Halabiyeh
food.desc: Aleppo claims dozens of kibbeh forms: fried torpedoes, baked trays, quince-stewed kibbeh safarjaliyeh and yoghurt-poached kibbeh labaniyeh.

places.name: Al-Kommeh
places.note: Known for reviving rarer kibbeh variations rather than only the fried version.

places.name: Beit Sissi
places.note: Reliable place to try kibbeh safarjaliyeh in quince sauce when in season.

places.name: Souq al-Zarb cookshops
places.note: Rebuilt souq lane with small kitchens turning out fried kibbeh through the day.

food.name: Sujuk and Basturma
food.desc: Spiced Armenian-Aleppian cured meats: fiery sujuk sausage and fenugreek-crusted basturma, eaten fried with eggs or stuffed into bread.

places.name: Midan Armenian quarter shops
places.note: The historic Armenian district where family charcuterie shops cure sujuk and basturma.

places.name: Souq al-Saqatiyya
places.note: Restored butchers' souq, reopened after reconstruction, good for cured meats and grills.

places.name: Aziziyah breakfast cafes
places.note: Central district cafes serving sujuk-and-egg pans at breakfast.

food.name: Foul and Fatteh Breakfast
food.desc: The Aleppo morning ritual: stewed fava beans with cumin and olive oil, or chickpea fatteh layered with yoghurt, ghee and toasted bread.

places.name: Abou Abdo Al-Fawal
places.note: Generations-old foul house, one of the city's best-known breakfast institutions.

places.name: Old City souq breakfast stalls
places.note: Early-morning fatteh and foul counters inside the rebuilt covered souq.

places.name: Aziziyah breakfast cafes
places.note: Easier sit-down option in the modern centre if you want a table and coffee.

food.name: Mabroumeh and Aleppo Pastries
food.desc: Aleppo is Syria's pastry capital: coiled pistachio mabroumeh, shredded balloriyeh and semolina karabij crowned with natef cream.

places.name: Hallab sweets
places.note: Aleppo sweets dynasty founded in 1881, the name most associated with mabroumeh.

places.name: Al-Telal Street sweet shops
places.note: Street lined with pastry houses; boxes are sold by weight and freshly cut.

places.name: Souq al-Madina confectioners
places.note: Reopened souq stalls selling karabij, halawet and nut-heavy pastries.

food.name: Sharab Tamer Hindi (Tamarind Drink)
food.desc: Chilled sweet-sour tamarind syrup poured over ice, sold from brass-urn vendors and shops; a Ramadan staple drunk all summer long.

places.name: Souq al-Madina drink vendors
places.note: Traditional brass-urn sellers work the rebuilt souq lanes and the citadel approach.

places.name: Bazerbashi
places.note: Long-running Aleppo ice cream and cold drinks house, good for tamarind and jallab.

places.name: Al-Telal Street juice bars
places.note: Row of juice counters mixing tamarind, jallab and fresh seasonal fruit.

food.name: Arabic Coffee with Cardamom
food.desc: Dark, thick, heavily cardamomed coffee served in tiny cups; Aleppo also roasts and grinds its own blends sold by the bag in the souq.

places.name: Aziziyah coffee houses
places.note: Central district cafes where the city's coffee-and-argileh culture regrouped after the war.

places.name: Souq al-Attarine roasters
places.note: Spice-souq roasters grind cardamom-heavy blends to order.

places.name: Beit Wakil courtyard
places.note: Quiet stone courtyard for an unhurried coffee after a mezze lunch.

landmarks: Citadel of Aleppo
One of the world's oldest and largest castles, this vast fortified mound has dominated the city for millennia, its Ayyubid gateway a masterpiece of medieval defence.
Al-Madina Souq
The world's largest covered historic market, kilometres of vaulted stone alleys trading silk, soap, and spices since the 14th century, now steadily being restored.
Great Umayyad Mosque of Aleppo
The city's holiest mosque, founded in 715 and famed for its courtyard and Seljuk minaret, undergoing painstaking reconstruction after wartime damage.
Khan al-Jumruk
The grandest of Aleppo's caravanserais, a 1574 customs khan whose massive courtyard once hosted English, Dutch, and French trading consulates.
Aleppo National Museum
Syria's treasure-house of the ancient Near East, guarded by colossal basalt statues from Tell Halaf and rich in Ebla and Mari artefacts.
Al-Jdeideh Quarter
The historic Christian quarter's lanes of 17th-century courtyard mansions, boutique museums, and churches embody Aleppo's famed cosmopolitan soul.
Forty Martyrs Armenian Cathedral
A 15th-century Armenian cathedral in Jdeideh, one of the oldest active churches in the diaspora and anchor of Aleppo's Armenian community.
Beit Ghazaleh
One of Aleppo's finest Ottoman-era courtyard palaces, its carved stone iwans and painted ceilings showcasing the opulence of 17th-century merchant families.
Bab Qinnasrin
The best-preserved of Aleppo's medieval city gates, a monumental 13th-century bastion guarding the old city's southern approach.
Church of Saint Simeon Stylites (Qalaat Samaan)
A day-trip Byzantine pilgrimage complex built around the pillar where Saint Simeon preached for 37 years, once Christendom's greatest church.

dom.op: Chemins de Fer Syriens (CFS) - tickets sold at the station counter only; there is no public online booking

train.note: Syrian Railways is headquartered in Aleppo but the network has barely functioned since services were suspended in 2012 - only around 1,050 km of the 2,750 km system is usable, and a test train between Aleppo and Hama in August 2025 was the first move towards restoring the Damascus-Aleppo line. Any passenger service that runs is sparse, changeable and sold at the station on the day rather than online, so treat the train as an opportunity rather than a plan. The international link north to Gaziantep in Turkey has been closed throughout the war, the Lebanese connection has been shut since the 1970s, and the narrow-gauge Hejaz route to Jordan is dormant despite a 2025 preliminary agreement to rebuild a stretch of it. Road transport is far quicker and more reliable in every direction.

intl.to: Beirut & Tripoli (Lebanon) - via the Dabbousiyeh and Masnaa crossings
intl.op: Al-Kadmous, Al-Ahliah and other Syrian coach companies - tickets at the international bus station counters

intl.to: Gaziantep, Antakya & Istanbul (Turkey) - via the Bab al-Hawa and Bab al-Salameh crossings
intl.op: Turkish and Syrian coach operators - tickets at the international bus station counters

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the international bus station (karaj) on the western side of Aleppo, a short taxi ride from the centre; company kiosks inside sell seats for cash and there is no dependable online booking, so buy a day or two ahead for popular departures. Damascus is 4-5 hrs down the M5 and Latakia 3-4 hrs to the west. Cross-border services to Lebanon and to Turkish cities have been running since the crossings reopened, but timetables, fares and which border is usable change frequently, and most nationalities need a Syrian visa arranged in advance. Check your government's current advice before travelling: much of Syria still carries a do-not-travel warning and conditions on the ground shift quickly.

ferry.note: Aleppo lies about 100 km inland with no navigable river, so there is no ferry service. The nearest ports are Latakia and Tartus, each 3-4 hrs away by road, and both are cargo harbours with no scheduled international passenger sailings.

half.name: Dead Cities (Serjilla and Al-Bara)
half.blurb: Abandoned Byzantine-era stone villages scattered across limestone hills, remarkably intact ruins of houses, tombs, and churches.

half.name: Hama
half.blurb: City on the Orontes River famous for its giant wooden norias, medieval waterwheels that still creak as they turn.

full.name: Krak des Chevaliers
full.blurb: One of the world's best-preserved Crusader castles, a massive fortress perched on a hilltop overlooking the Homs Gap.
